claim: Cancer is a clonal evolutionary process, caused by successive accumulation of genetic alterations providing milestones of tumor initiation, progression, dissemination, and/or resistance to certain therapeutic regimes.
source: Cancer is a clonal evolutionary process, caused by successive accumulation of genetic alterations providing milestones of tumor initiation, progression, dissemination, and/or resistance to certain therapeutic regimes.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: The evolution of CLL follows a time-ordered process represented as a global flow in TEDG that proceeds from initiating events to late events.
source: (a) the evolution of CLL follows a time-ordered process represented as a global flow in TEDG that proceeds from initiating events to late events
evidence: This claim is supported by the TEDG analysis performed on the CLL cohort data.

claim: There are two distinct and mutually exclusive evolutionary paths of CLL evolution.
source: (b) there are two distinct and mutually exclusive evolutionary paths of CLL evolution
evidence: This claim is supported by the TEDG analysis and statistical association analysis of the CLL cohort.

claim: Higher fitness clones are present in later stages of the disease, indicating a progressive clonal replacement with more aggressive clones.
source: (c) higher fitness clones are present in later stages of the disease, indicating a progressive clonal replacement with more aggressive clones
evidence: This claim is supported by the growth rate analysis of genetic lesions in the CLL cohort.

claim: Cancer is a complex, Darwinian, adaptive clonal evolutionary process, driven by the accumulation of genetic alterations that confer high proliferative and survival advantage.
source: Cancer is a complex, Darwinian, adaptive clonal evolutionary process, driven by the accumulation of genetic alterations that confer high proliferative and survival advantage (Merlo et al., 2006; Greaves and Maley, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent advances in sequencing technologies have allowed uncovering the most common genetic alterations of many tumors.
source: Recent advances in sequencing technologies have allowed uncovering the most common genetic alterations of many tumors, but the temporal order of most of these alterations is still unknown (Futreal et al., 2004; Greenman et al., 2007; Santarius et al., 2010; Lawrence et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The temporal order of most genetic alterations in tumors is still unknown.
source: Recent advances in sequencing technologies have allowed uncovering the most common genetic alterations of many tumors, but the temporal order of most of these alterations is still unknown (Futreal et al., 2004; Greenman et al., 2007; Santarius et al., 2010; Lawrence et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Landau et al. sampled leukemia cells from 18 CLL patients at two time points, revealing that SF3B1 and TP53 mutations are late events in subclonal tumor cells.
source: Landau et al. sampled leukemia cells from 18 CLL patients at two time points, revealing that SF3B1 and TP53 mutations are late events in subclonal tumor cells (Landau et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The study of different stages of colorectal carcinogenesis showed the sequence of genetic events to be APC, KRAS, and then TP53.
source: The study of different stages of colorectal carcinogenesis showed the sequence of genetic events to be APC, KRAS, and then TP53 (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RESIC is a stochastic process model to identify the order of mutations.
source: RESIC is a stochastic process model to identify the order of mutations (Attolini et al., 2010), which successfully confirmed the results in colorectal cancer, suggesting that cross-sectional data is informative for the prediction of mutation order.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RESIC successfully confirmed the results in colorectal cancer, suggesting that cross-sectional data is informative for the prediction of mutation order.
source: RESIC is a stochastic process model to identify the order of mutations (Attolini et al., 2010), which successfully confirmed the results in colorectal cancer, suggesting that cross-sectional data is informative for the prediction of mutation order.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RESIC does not consider a critical aspect of carcinogenesis that most tumors are heterogeneous.
source: However, RESIC does not consider a critical aspect of carcinogenesis that most tumors are heterogeneous (Parsons, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CLL represents the most common adult leukemia in Western countries.
source: In this study, we have applied TEDG to study the dynamics of the acquisition of alterations in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), which represents the most common adult leukemia in Western countries (Hallek et al., 2008; Müller-Hermelink et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CLL is an ideal model for studying clonal dynamics because it is possible to collect highly purified sequential samples over time.
source: CLL is an ideal model for studying clonal dynamics because it is possible to collect highly purified sequential samples over time, and its clinical course is well characterized by serial cycles of response, remissions, and relapse ending in some instances with the development of lethal complications such as chemoresistant progression or transformation into an aggressive lymphoma (Richter syndrome) (Pasqualucci et al., 2011; Zenz et al., 2012; Fabbri et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The clinical course of CLL is well characterized by serial cycles of response, remissions, and relapse ending in some instances with the development of lethal complications such as chemoresistant progression or transformation into an aggressive lymphoma (Richter syndrome).
source: CLL is an ideal model for studying clonal dynamics because it is possible to collect highly purified sequential samples over time, and its clinical course is well characterized by serial cycles of response, remissions, and relapse ending in some instances with the development of lethal complications such as chemoresistant progression or transformation into an aggressive lymphoma (Richter syndrome) (Pasqualucci et al., 2011; Zenz et al., 2012; Fabbri et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study collected genomic information from the most common alterations in a cohort of 70 CLL patients spanning over a period of 12 years (2001–2012).
source: For this purpose, we envision a dual cross-sectional and longitudinal strategy by collecting genomic information from the most common alterations in a cohort of 70 CLL patients spanning over a period of 12 years (2001–2012).
evidence: This statement describes the data collection for the study.

claim: Half (35 out of 70) of the patients have at least one subclonal genetic lesion with mutation frequency less than 20% at diagnosis.
source: Half (35 out of 70) of the patients have at least one subclonal genetic lesion with mutation frequency less than 20% at diagnosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: If the genetic alterations driving CLL progression follow a preferential order, there exists a well ordered directed flow in ISN.
source: We ask whether the genetic lesions in CLL are temporally ordered or randomly accumulated and reason that if the genetic alterations driving CLL progression follow a preferential order, there exists a well ordered directed flow in ISN.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the TEDG framework.

claim: Figure 3A represents a hierarchical layout of ISN, which depicts an ordered structure of lesions in genes represented by sources (nodes with more outgoing arrows) and sinks (nodes with more incoming arrows) (p-value < 0.0001, chi square distribution).
source: Figure 3A represents a hierarchical layout of ISN, which depicts an ordered structure of lesions in genes represented by sources (nodes with more outgoing arrows) and sinks (nodes with more incoming arrows) (p-value < 0.0001, chi square distribution).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the ISN shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletion of 13q14, +12 and mutations of NOTCH1 are significant early events in CLL development.
source: Deletion of 13q14, +12 and mutations of NOTCH1 are significant early events in CLL development, while mutations of TP53 and BIRC3 are significant late events.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal order analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutations of TP53 and BIRC3 are significant late events in CLL development.
source: Deletion of 13q14, +12 and mutations of NOTCH1 are significant early events in CLL development, while mutations of TP53 and BIRC3 are significant late events.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal order analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MYD88 mutations might occur even before 13q14 deletion (one of six patients), indicating that activation of the Toll-like receptor pathway could be important in the initiation of a fraction of CLL tumors.
source: Though the sample size prevents statistical considerations, MYD88 mutations might occur even before 13q14 deletion (one of six patients), indicating that activation of the Toll-like receptor pathway could be important in the initiation of a fraction of CLL tumors (Arvaniti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the study and supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The sequential order of the genetic lesions remains consistent (Pearson's correlation = 0.9, p-value < 1e-3) when evolutionary networks are constructed with patients who received chemotherapy.
source: The sequential order of the genetic lesions remains consistent (Pearson's correlation = 0.9, p-value < 1e-3) when evolutionary networks are constructed with patients who received chemotherapy (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the order of development of the genetic lesions may be affected by therapy (the Pearson's correlation of the order in patients without chemotherapy is 0.4 with p-value > 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The order of development of the genetic lesions may be affected by therapy.
source: The sequential order of the genetic lesions remains consistent (Pearson's correlation = 0.9, p-value < 1e-3) when evolutionary networks are constructed with patients who received chemotherapy (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the order of development of the genetic lesions may be affected by therapy (the Pearson's correlation of the order in patients without chemotherapy is 0.4 with p-value > 0.1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The monoallelic 13q14 deletion, RB1 deletion, and +12 are significant early events (p-value < 0.01).
source: We observe that the monoallelic 13q14 deletion, RB1 deletion, and +12 are significant early events (p-value < 0.01), while the BIRC3 E537fs and the TP53 R248Q are significant late lesions (p-value < 0.05) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BIRC3 E537fs and the TP53 R248Q are significant late lesions (p-value < 0.05).
source: We observe that the monoallelic 13q14 deletion, RB1 deletion, and +12 are significant early events (p-value < 0.01), while the BIRC3 E537fs and the TP53 R248Q are significant late lesions (p-value < 0.05) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different lesions affecting the same gene may occur in distinct branches and stages.
source: Also, the analysis of ISN and TEDG shows that different lesions affecting the same gene may occur in distinct branches and stages.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of ISN and TEDG.

claim: Mutations K700E and K666E of SF3B1 are late events in cases harboring 13q14 deletion.
source: For example, mutations K700E and K666E of SF3B1 are late events in cases harboring 13q14 deletion, while mutations R273C of TP53 are late events in cases with +12.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of ISN and TEDG.

claim: Mutations R273C of TP53 are late events in cases with +12.
source: For example, mutations K700E and K666E of SF3B1 are late events in cases harboring 13q14 deletion, while mutations R273C of TP53 are late events in cases with +12.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of ISN and TEDG.

claim: TEDG reveals the H179R and Y234C missense substitutions in TP53 may be early events, while the R248Q, R273C, P152fs, and N239T substitutions are late events.
source: Though the sample size prevents statistical considerations, TEDG reveals the H179R and Y234C missense substitutions in TP53 may be early events, while the R248Q, R273C, P152fs, and N239T substitutions are late events.
evidence: This claim is based on the TEDG analysis, but the sample size limits statistical power.

claim: A minority of patients (n = 3/60, 5%; FDR = 0.1) are characterized by a significantly decreased or undetectable representation of the founding clone, coupled with a significant increase of a second subclone that represented a small subpopulation at an earlier time point, consistent with a branching evolution model.
source: The analysis of our cohort (excluding patients with Richter's transformation, refer to 'Materials and methods' for details) shows that a minority of patients (n = 3/60, 5%; FDR = 0.1) are characterized by a significantly decreased or undetectable representation of the founding clone, coupled with a significant increase of a second subclone that represented a small subpopulation at an earlier time point, consistent with a branching evolution model (highlighted by yellow circle in Figure 5A–B, and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 1.

claim: In all three cases clonal replacement events involve SF3B1 mutations and occur after treatment.
source: Interestingly, in all three cases clonal replacement events involve SF3B1 mutations and occur after treatment (Figure 5C), suggesting that the branching evolution model is closely connected to the combination of treatments and the emergence of SF3B1 mutations (p-value = 0.0016 by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The branching evolution model is closely connected to the combination of treatments and the emergence of SF3B1 mutations (p-value = 0.0016 by Fisher's exact test).
source: Interestingly, in all three cases clonal replacement events involve SF3B1 mutations and occur after treatment (Figure 5C), suggesting that the branching evolution model is closely connected to the combination of treatments and the emergence of SF3B1 mutations (p-value = 0.0016 by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At the time of treatment requirement, limiting the knowledge of disease genetics to the dominant clone will likely be uninformative for accurate therapeutic decisions.
source: This observation implies that, at the time of treatment requirement, limiting the knowledge of disease genetics to the dominant clone will likely be uninformative for accurate therapeutic decisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of clonal replacement events.

claim: Most of the co-mutations are experimentally confirmed by previous studies, including: co-occurrence of 17p13 deletion and TP53 mutations, reflecting a typical two-hit model for tumor suppressor genes; co-occurrence of BIRC3 deletion, 11q22-q23 deletion, and BIRC3 mutations; and the relationship between NOTCH1 mutations and +12.
source: Most of the co-mutations (connected in red in Figure 6B) are experimentally confirmed by previous studies, including: co-occurrence of 17p13 deletion and TP53 mutations, reflecting a typical two-hit model for tumor suppressor genes; co-occurrence of BIRC3 deletion, 11q22-q23 deletion, and BIRC3 mutations; and the relationship between NOTCH1 mutations and +12 (Balatti et al., 2012; Del Giudice et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: This large cohort of patients allows the statistical power to reveal other significant and previously unreported co-occurrence interactions, including the co-occurrence of BIRC3 abnormalities with +12 and NOTCH1 mutations and the co-occurrence of 13q14 deletion and BIRC3 deletion.
source: In addition to previously reported associated lesions, this large cohort of patients allows the statistical power to reveal other significant and previously unreported co-occurrence interactions, including the co-occurrence of BIRC3 abnormalities with +12 and NOTCH1 mutations and the co-occurrence of 13q14 deletion and BIRC3 deletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the large cohort.

claim: This large cohort also reveals mutually exclusive relationships between +12 and 13q14 deletion and between NOTCH1 mutations and 13q14 deletion.
source: This large cohort also reveals mutually exclusive relationships between +12 and 13q14 deletion and between NOTCH1 mutations and 13q14 deletion (connected in blue in Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The statistical association analysis is consistent with the prediction of TEDG and indirectly validates the ability of TEDG in successfully capturing the major information in tumor evolution.
source: The statistical association analysis is consistent with the prediction of TEDG and indirectly validates the ability of TEDG in successfully capturing the major information in tumor evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency between TEDG predictions and statistical association analysis.

claim: The growth rates of late events (17p13 deletion, mutations of SF3B1, 11q22-q23 deletion, BIRC3 deletion, mutations of TP53, and mutations of BIRC3) are found higher than those of early events (mutations of MYD88, 13q14 deletion, +12, mutations of NOTCH1, and RB1 deletion) with p-value = 0.005 by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test.
source: Interestingly, the growth rates of late events (17p13 deletion, mutations of SF3B1, 11q22-q23 deletion, BIRC3 deletion, mutations of TP53, and mutations of BIRC3) are found higher than those of early events (mutations of MYD88, 13q14 deletion, +12, mutations of NOTCH1, and RB1 deletion) with p-value = 0.005 by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Figure 6C), revealing that late events may drive higher fitness or more aggressive clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Late events may drive higher fitness or more aggressive clones.
source: Interestingly, the growth rates of late events (17p13 deletion, mutations of SF3B1, 11q22-q23 deletion, BIRC3 deletion, mutations of TP53, and mutations of BIRC3) are found higher than those of early events (mutations of MYD88, 13q14 deletion, +12, mutations of NOTCH1, and RB1 deletion) with p-value = 0.005 by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Figure 6C), revealing that late events may drive higher fitness or more aggressive clones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth rate analysis.

claim: After eliminating clonal genetic lesions with MCF > 20% in the above analysis, the growth rates of late and early events are still significantly different with p-value = 0.0114 by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test.
source: However, after eliminating clonal genetic lesions with MCF > 20% in the above analysis, we still find the growth rates of late and early events to be significantly different with p-value = 0.0114 by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only genetic lesions affecting the TP53 gene show a statistically significant association with MMFS (p-value = 0.0164, by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test).
source: In our cohort, only genetic lesions affecting the TP53 gene show a statistically significant association with MMFS (p-value = 0.0164, by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the cohort data.

claim: The fastest-growing clones are strongly correlated with poor survival and Richter syndrome transformation.
source: Clinically, the fastest-growing clones are strongly correlated with poor survival and Richter syndrome transformation, consistent with the fact that CLL transformed to Richter syndrome presents significantly higher MMFS values (p-value = 0.002, by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CLL transformed to Richter syndrome presents significantly higher MMFS values (p-value = 0.002, by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test).
source: Clinically, the fastest-growing clones are strongly correlated with poor survival and Richter syndrome transformation, consistent with the fact that CLL transformed to Richter syndrome presents significantly higher MMFS values (p-value = 0.002, by Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Having a clone with high MMFS associates with an approximately threefold significant increase in the hazard of death (HR: 3.17; 95% CI: 1.38–7.40; p-value = 0.005) and a significant shortening of overall survival (47% at 5 years).
source: Indeed, by survival analysis, having a clone with high MMFS associates with an approximately threefold significant increase in the hazard of death (HR: 3.17; 95% CI: 1.38–7.40; p-value = 0.005) and a significant shortening of overall survival (47% at 5 years) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most deaths (77%) in patients carrying a clone with high MMFS are due to Richter syndrome transformation.
source: Most deaths (77%) in patients carrying a clone with high MMFS are due to Richter syndrome transformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the cohort.

claim: Patients having a clone with high MMFS show an approximately fourfold increased risk of Richter syndrome development (HR: 4.61; 95% CI: 1.54–13.80; p-value = 0.003) and an ∼50% of them are projected to develop Richter syndrome at 5 years.
source: Consistently, patients having a clone with high MMFS show an approximately fourfold increased risk of Richter syndrome development (HR: 4.61; 95% CI: 1.54–13.80; p-value = 0.003) and an ∼50% of them are projected to develop Richter syndrome at 5 years (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The first evolutionary path involves CLL harboring +12 and NOTCH1 mutations as early driver events.
source: The first evolutionary path involves CLL harboring +12 and NOTCH1 mutations as early driver events. In this path, clonal evolution proceeds toward the development of TP53 and BIRC3 abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of TEDG topology and association analysis.

claim: In the first evolutionary path, clonal evolution proceeds toward the development of TP53 and BIRC3 abnormalities.
source: The first evolutionary path involves CLL harboring +12 and NOTCH1 mutations as early driver events. In this path, clonal evolution proceeds toward the development of TP53 and BIRC3 abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of TEDG topology and association analysis.

claim: The second evolutionary path involves 13q14 deletion as early driver lesion and proceeds toward the development of SF3B1 mutations and BIRC3 abnormalities.
source: The second evolutionary path involves 13q14 deletion as early driver lesion and proceeds toward the development of SF3B1 mutations and BIRC3 abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of TEDG topology and association analysis.

claim: The results are consistent with the different clinico-biological phenotype of +12 CLL and 13q14 deleted CLL and further support the hypothesis that at least two distinct genetic subtypes of CLL exist.
source: Overall, our results are consistent with the different clinico-biological phenotype of +12 CLL and 13q14 deleted CLL and further support the hypothesis that at least two distinct genetic subtypes of CLL exist.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TEDG analysis and association analysis.

claim: Deletion of 13q14 and +12 occur at a similar prevalence in all CLL phases, including monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, a condition that often anticipates overt CLL, thus suggesting that they are early events.
source: This observation is consistent with the notion that del13q and +12 occur at a similar prevalence in all CLL phases, including monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, a condition that often anticipates overt CLL, thus suggesting that they are early events (Rawstron et al., 2008; Nieto et al., 2009; Rossi et al., 2009b; Fazi et al., 2011; Pasqualucci et al., 2011; Kern et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 13q14 deletion has been directly implicated in CLL initiation.
source: Also, 13q14 deletion has been directly implicated in CLL initiation (Klein et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Late-onset abnormalities are known to accumulate in more advanced phases of the disease, thus suggesting that they are second-hit lesions.
source: On the other hand, late-onset abnormalities are known to accumulate in more advanced phases of the disease, thus suggesting that they are second-hit lesions (Zenz et al., 2009; Rossi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations of SF3B1 and 11q22-q23 deletions appear to be acquired at an intermediate time point.
source: In our model, mutations of SF3B1 and 11q22-q23 deletions appear to be acquired at an intermediate time point.
evidence: This claim is based on the TEDG analysis.

claim: This observation is consistent with the clinical observation that mutations of SF3B1 and 11q22-q23 deletion co-segregate with an intermediate prognostic group of CLL.
source: This observation is consistent with the clinical observation that mutations of SF3B1 and 11q22-q23 deletion co-segregate with an intermediate prognostic group of CLL (Döhner et al., 2000; Oscier et al., 2013; Rossi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Deletion of 13q14 and +12 are mutually exclusive in CLL.
source: Our data, as well as previous analyses (Rossi et al., 2013), show that deletion of 13q14 and +12 are mutually exclusive in CLL.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to previous research.

claim: +12 CLL is known to stand out of typical 13q14 deleted CLL because of their atypical cytomorphology and phenotype, the more intense expression of CD20, the preferential nodal presentation and the higher risk of transformation to Richter syndrome.
source: From a clinical standpoint, +12 CLL is known to stand out of typical 13q14 deleted CLL because of their atypical cytomorphology and phenotype, the more intense expression of CD20, the preferential nodal presentation and the higher risk of transformation to Richter syndrome.
evidence: This statement draws from established clinical knowledge.

claim: The presence at diagnosis of fully clonal genetic lesions that are considered late genetic events in CLL evolution, such as TP53 abnormalities, is already known to have an adverse impact on disease outcome.
source: The presence at diagnosis of fully clonal genetic lesions that are considered late genetic events in CLL evolution, such as TP53 abnormalities, is already known to have an adverse impact on disease outcome (Zenz et al., 2008, 2010; Dicker et al., 2009; Malcikova et al., 2009; Rossi et al., 2009a; Gonzalez et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A fraction of TP53 abnormalities, though subclonal at presentation, lead to expansion of fitter subclones that progressively predominate with time in the tumor architecture.
source: We observe that a fraction of TP53 abnormalities, though subclonal at presentation, lead to expansion of fitter subclones that progressively predominate with time in the tumor architecture.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis from the study.

claim: Harboring higher fitness alterations correlates with poor survival and increased risk of CLL transformation into an aggressive lymphoma.
source: The clinical impact of this observation is supported by the evidence that harboring higher fitness alterations correlates with poor survival and increased risk of CLL transformation into an aggressive lymphoma, an often-lethal complication known as Richter syndrome.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: The ATM gene is large and highly polymorphic without well-known hotspots.
source: The ATM mutations are also commonly found in CLL; however, the ATM gene is large and highly polymorphic without well-known hotspots.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the ATM gene.

claim: The distinction of ATM driver mutations from constitutional variants is challenging.
source: The ATM mutations are also commonly found in CLL; however, the ATM gene is large and highly polymorphic without well-known hotspots. Therefore, the distinction of its driver mutations from constitutional variants is challenging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the ATM gene.

claim: The prognostic relevance of ATM mutations in CLL is still controversial.
source: Also, from a clinical standpoint, the prognostic relevance of ATM mutations in CLL is still controversial, so we have excluded this gene from the current study (Lozanski et al., 2012; Ouillette et al., 2012; Skowronska et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TEDG is able to improve cancer classification and dissection into genetic subgroups following different paths of clonal evolution.
source: In conclusion, the application of TEDG to CLL provides the proof-of-principle that this method is able to: (i) improve cancer classification and dissection into genetic subgroups following different paths of clonal evolution
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results of the study.

claim: TEDG is able to anticipate the genetic composition of the progressive/relapsed disease according to the genetic composition of the tumor clone at the time of diagnosis, including the development of genetic lesions associated with chemorefractoriness.
source: (ii) anticipate the genetic composition of the progressive/relapsed disease according to the genetic composition of the tumor clone at the time of diagnosis, including the development of genetic lesions associated with chemorefractoriness.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results of the study.

claim: TEDG provides a general framework that could be used to study and compare the evolutionary histories of other tumors.
source: TEDG provides a general framework that could be used to study and compare the evolutionary histories of other tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applicability of TEDG.

claim: 70 out of the 202 patients were informative for TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, MYD88, or BIRC3 mutations (which are the most common mutations in this leukemia), overall accounting for 164 paired sequential samples collected at diagnosis, progression, and last follow-up.
source: 70 out of the 202 patients were informative for TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, MYD88, or BIRC3 mutations (which are the most common mutations in this leukemia), overall accounting for 164 paired sequential samples collected at diagnosis, progression, and last follow-up.
evidence: This statement describes the patient cohort used in the study.

claim: The study was approved by the institutional ethical committee of the Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Maggiore della Carità di Novara affiliated with the Amedeo Avogadro University of Eastern Piedmont, Novara, Italy (Protocol Code 59/CE; Study Number CE 8/11).
source: The study was approved by the institutional ethical committee of the Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Maggiore della Carità di Novara affiliated with the Amedeo Avogadro University of Eastern Piedmont, Novara, Italy (Protocol Code 59/CE; Study Number CE 8/11).
evidence: This statement describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Patients provided informed consent in accordance with local IRB requirements and Declaration of Helsinki.
source: Patients provided informed consent in accordance with local IRB requirements and Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This statement describes the informed consent process.

claim: In all cases, the fraction of tumor cells corresponded to 70–98% as assessed by flow cytometry.
source: In all cases, the fraction of tumor cells corresponded to 70–98% as assessed by flow cytometry.
evidence: This statement describes the tumor purity of the samples.

claim: The sequencing depth in this study is on average 1200×, which is sufficient for a highly sensitive detection of mutations with allele frequency >1% out of the background error noise.
source: The sequencing depth in this study is on average 1200×, which is sufficient for a highly sensitive detection of mutations with allele frequency >1% out of the background error noise (Rossi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes the sequencing depth and is supported by a citation.

claim: With 30 patients, TEDG's accuracy for a linear model is 80%, and for a branching model, it reaches 90%.
source: With 30 patients, TEDG's accuracy for a linear model is 80%, and for a branching model, it reaches 90% (Figure 2E–G, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The optimal value of β is related to the number of samples, but the wide range of high accuracy region suggests that the TEDG results are robust to the parameter selection.
source: Figure 2C indicates that the optimal value of β is related to the number of samples, but the wide range of high accuracy region suggests that the TEDG results are robust to the parameter selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TEDG proceeds in two steps to ensemble in a simplified way cancer clonal evolutionary histories of large number of patients: first, by merging the evolutionary history of each patient, and second, by removing indirect relationships using spectral techniques for network deconvolution.
source: Our method, termed tumor evolutionary directed graphs (TEDG), proceeds in two steps to ensemble in a simplified way cancer clonal evolutionary histories of large number of patients: first, by merging the evolutionary history of each patient, and second, by removing indirect relationships using spectral techniques for network deconvolution (Feizi et al., 2013).
